utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we will hear the testimony of the next witness, I would like to briefly into turn private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber understands that the objections against paragraph 12 of the statement of the witness have been withdrawn by the Prosecution through an informal communication, but it's hereby on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vujicic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujicic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vujicic, we were informed that you may have some difficulties now and then in hearing, and that this would especially apply --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- when there is an overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Especially -- precisely. Precisely. When people speak to me in a foreign language, then it is being conveyed to me into the Serbian language that I speak and then a bit of it is lost, so technically speaking, could this please be taken into account? Could at least a sentence be uttered to me in the foreign language that is spoken and then I hear the interpretation into Serbian? I think I will actually speed things up that way so I don't have to ask for the question to be repeated to me once again. Right this very instant, I can hear it well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, it may not always be possible to wait with the translation until after the question has been put, but if ever you have any difficulties in understanding or in hearing, please raise your hand, draw my attention to it, and we'll accommodate you in whatever way, most likely by repeating the question. At the same time I invite the parties to avoid any overlap which may confuse the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vujicic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is to your left. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could have in e-court the 65 ter number 1D01658.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you can please look at the signature on the first page of this statement and tell me if you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I recognise this. This is my statement. This is my signature. The one that I made personally, in respect of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to the last page of the document in the original Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you will see a signature there as well. Can you tell us whose signature this is?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: This is my signature personally, my statement that conscientiously, without being talked into anything by anyone, that I personally gave this statement and signed it on the 5th of June 2014.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, after signing this statement, did you have occasion to review the same in the Serbian language to verify its accuracy?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I checked it and it is exactly the way I gave it, the first time I gave it. And as far as I'm concerned, it can be admitted into evidence in this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We will get to that, sir. First of all, I have to ask you, do you stand behind everything that is written in your statement as being accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I stand by that, everything that I was in a position to say then. And I'm also giving the possibility to everyone to put additional questions to me. I am prepared to answer all questions that you may have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, if I were to ask you questions today about the same topics as covered in your statement, would your answers be the same in substance as is already contained in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And given that you have taken the solemn declaration to tell the truth, would those answers as contained in your written statement be truthful?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've already said that I will speak the truth the whole truth and nothing but the truth, and I will do my best to speak the truth. I will speak about what I know. And if somebody asks me questions about what I had not seen with my own eyes but that I had just heard about, I cannot guarantee about that. I mean, in respect of such questions, I can say that I heard something, even if I hadn't seen it with my very own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender 1D01658 into evidence under Rule 92 ter at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1658 receives number D579, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would read the public summary of the witness's statement, which has been explained to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please read the summary, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The witness stated that in the first half of April 1992, the civilian authorities of Foca decided to start a shelter for Muslim women from Foca in the Partizan sports club. This was because Foca was a scattered geographic community and the authorities were unable to maintain control and ensure security for the civilian population of outlying villages. This was styled a reception centre. In one such centre 150 metres from the witness's home, he was engaged to provide armed security with a rifle for four nights. He was given the task of not allowing anyone to enter the premises during his shift. Several women were at this facility. The women were free to move in and out of the facility, and during the time period he was a guard there, there were no incidents. The witness does know that in other places, the houses of Muslims were protected by guards also sent by the civilian authorities. He knows of one incident where a guard at a house of the Rikali family tried to stop a paramilitary member from entering the house and shot and killed that paramilitary. The witness says the first shots fired and the first house burned in Foca when the conflict broke out were acts done by Muslims. The mosques were used to store large caches of weapons and a Bosnian Muslim sniper fired from the minaret of the Aladza mosque. The Aladza mosque was not damaged or destroyed during the first clashes and was barricaded and taped off until August 1992 when unknown individuals blew off explosives in that mosque. This explosion damaged 50 buildings in the vicinity of the mosque whose owners were mostly Serbs. That completes the public summary of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. If you have any further questions to the witness, please put them to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to ask a few questions about your statement. If we can turn to page 2 in both languages, and if we can focus on paragraphs 4 through 9 of the same, and, sir, here you talk about providing security for four nights to a facility that was 150 metres from your home. Can you please identify by name that facility so we know exactly what it is you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That facility was called the sports centre Partizan. It was a recreation sports centre for young people. It had a big hall inside, and also some auxiliary premises like bathrooms and so on. Also some small offices. These premises were used in the second half of April 1992 when -- you know, the municipality of Foca is the largest municipality in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were lots of villages. It was very big. The villages were scattered all about. The authorities could not control each and every house. And in these houses, after the cleansing and after the clashes and after the removal of the Green Berets and this Patriotic League, some families remained unprotected, including women, frail old men, et cetera. The civilian and military authorities, or rather this Territorial Defence issued an order as follows: Whenever such structures and families are under threat, they should come to a single place where they could stay, and these women were accommodated right there at Partizan. When they arrived there during those first days, the territorial or rather, no, the Crisis Staff of this Territorial Defence issued an order to protect this facility, day and night. For four nights, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, finish your answer.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: All right. For four nights, I stood guard with the rifle in my hands. Some commissioner from the Crisis Staff gave me a rifle, issued an order saying that we should not allow anyone in during the night. If anybody tries to enter by force, that we should stop them, even physically. However, fortunately, during those four nights, I was not on my own totally. There was this other man on one side, and all of this security was there so that nobody could come. So it was safe. Nobody came so we did not have a problem. After that, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, we have much of that in your statement. I'm limited with time. I would please like to ask questions and get your answers to them so we may proceed. Now, at the time that you were providing security for the Partizan sports centre, what was your status? Were you part of either the police or the military or something else?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I was a civilian, and during the pre-war period, I was president of the Gornje Polje local commune where this facility is. So I was a civilian. And as for my age, according to the then-regulations, I was not even a military conscript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What can you tell us about the provision of food and water for those persons that were inside the facility?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I know that these persons were provided for. Somewhere there was a kitchen at the hotel and food was being brought to them, and during the day they had the opportunity of going down to the hotel and having lunch, dinner, et cetera. During the night they were closed up. They had a key on the inside; they were locked in. While I was there, I knew that women were there. I never saw a single one of these women. I never opened the door; I never even took the doorknob into my hands. That's what I can say. I can also say that during the day, these women had the opportunity of leaving, going out on visits. There were Muslim women there and then they knew some Serb women from town, and they would see each other. But during the night, that is what I'm telling you, nobody came by.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've identified that during the night they were closed up. They had a key on the inside; they were locked in. Who is "they" that had the key to the Partizan sports facility during the nights?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Who they were?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Who had the key?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: They, the women, they locked up during the night and then during the day they could go out for walks in town, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During the four nights that you provided security, how did you obtain food and eat?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: There was a woman there in the same facility, on the other side, all by herself, this woman, and once, one night, two nights, she prepared food for us because we did not -- we could not leave that facility at all. My apartment was about 150 metres away from that facility and I didn't dare leave, go have dinner at home or breakfast at home, until the people from the other shift would come in. I don't know about the day-time shifts, especially from the moment when I was mobilised into the Territorial Defence units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We will get to your mobilisation. I'd like to first ask you, how did you regard those persons that were inside the facility? Were they your prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: No. This was -- may I start now? This was just a reception centre. They were free women, like all Muslim and Serb women in the town of Foca, except that they had had come from the villages in order to be safe in one particular place so they could be protected properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of any incidents occurring at that location, the Partizan sports club, where people from the outside came and repeatedly mistreated these civilian women who were inside the hall?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: After I left, I really did not hear about any incidents. Also, my wife, who was nearby, 100 or 150 metres away, she never told me about any such thing. I was at the front-line, you see, but she never told me about any accidents during the day or during the night. There is nothing more I can tell you except for this: I had been mobilised, so I would return every 15 days it in order to get a change of clothes, et cetera, so please don't ask me any more about this because I really don't know. I have nothing more to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Looking at paragraph 8 of your statement, you say that Muslims began to leave Foca. Did any Muslims also stay in Foca?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Many Muslims, after the conflict broke out, left Foca together with -- and withdrew together with the Green Berets and the Patriotic League towards Gorazde, towards Ustikolina. Most of them. That has been recorded. And a good part of the families of Muslim ethnicity remained in town. All summer they lived as they wished and the civilian authorities, when they applied for leaving, always told them, "There is no need for you to leave. You can stay. You will be safe like all other citizens in the Foca area." And when they left, they always left on the pretext that they wanted to reunite with their families, probably with those who had left before or those who had left with the units of these Green Berets and the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in the same paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I apologise. And many of them in fact remained throughout the time of the conflict until 1995, and there were some of them who even were in units of the territorial units. And after June, when the VRS was organised, they actually joined the units of the Army of Republika Srpska and discharged specific duties there. I can tell you their names, if need -- if necessary. I can name a few by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You have identified in paragraph 8 and today that you were mobilised. Into what formation were you mobilised? Was this the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: At that time, the Crisis Staff was active and the Territorial Defence, they were the army. That was April. And the Army of Republika Srpska was set up only after June, perhaps in the first half of July. But until that time, it was a Territorial Defence that was active comprising these units of so-called village guards who were gathered, rallied and so on. The army was organised, two brigades were organised in July, the 11th and the 12th Light Infantry Brigade, and of course the officers at the orders of the commander Marko Kovac. Until that time we had a Territorial Defence which consisted of people who had rifles in their arms but they were civilians in civilian clothing and they had no equipment to speak of. These were people with rifle in hand, infantry weapons. Even when the army of the Republika Srpska was formed up, it was the Light Infantry Brigade, which actually meant that they had infantry rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: After you were mobilised, did you at any time receive instruction in the laws of war and how to deal with enemy prisoners and civilians encountered during combat?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: On several occasions, as people got mobilised, they would be lined up in front of the secondary school centre. I was in one of those lineups. I was engaged as a combatant. They read to us the conventions on international war law and I had been familiar with those in view of my profession already. And they literally read out everything which is in the conventions, namely how a fighter, a soldier, should conduct himself, how the officers should behave, how the population should be protected. And there should be no torching, no killing. And if there were prisoners of war taken prisoner as fighters, there could be no summary judgements. They should be put on trial, their responsibility actually investigated, and that was all read out to us. It was not only read out to me; it was read out to the entire lineup. I was standing at attention as that was being read.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could I seek clarification on two matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First you said you were familiar with the laws of war in view of your profession. Your profession at that time was what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a jurist. Now I'm a pensioner, so I learned about laws of war during my studies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My second question is: Did you learn that prisoners of war should be put on trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No trials were conducted of civilians at all. If they were brought into places, they were there to be protected. But those who torched Serbian villages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- there were no trials. There is not a single judgement in Foca handed down to anyone, not the members of the Green Berets or the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I give you a signal to stop, please stop talking. My question was and I read to you what you initially said: "There should be no torching, no killing. And if there were prisoners of war taken prisoner as fighters, there could be no summary judgements. They should be put on trial." Do I understand that you learned that prisoners of war taken prisoner as fighters should be put on trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not what I said. There was not a single judgement to such persons. They would be brought in. Perhaps they were subjected to investigation, but there were no judgements, there were no trials conducted against such persons. Against such persons, I don't know about that. I know that there were no trials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was not asking whether there were trials but whether you were taught that prisoners of war should be put at trial. Whether it happened is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. When these regulations, laws of war and these conventions were being read out to us, it was never said that they would be put on trial but that they would be treated in compliance with the rules of the laws of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, there may be a translation issue, but what I just read to the witness sounds different. If there is any translation issue, please let the Chamber know. Otherwise, we'll -- and then of course we will verify it. If not, however, then we'll just take it that the witness said what is on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, at paragraphs -- you have two paragraph 10s in your statement, both of which occur at pages 2 to 3 in the English and 2 to 3 in the Serbian, and in both paragraphs you mention paramilitaries. Where did these paramilitaries come from?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, frankly speaking, I don't exactly know where they came from. They crossed the borders with Montenegro, with Serbia, and from some parts of Croatia, and via Dubrovnik and so. But who they were, what they were, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What were they doing in Foca? What kind of activities?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: There was not an order of the Crisis Staff or the Territorial Defence that they acted upon. They came of their own accord. They were independent in their actions. And when the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Foca had put things in order and when peace prevailed in the city, the focus shifted to the villages, and these units were more in the villages as of then.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did they cause any problems with the local population?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They did cause problems, both for Serbs and for the Muslim population in a specific way. Well, to tell you frankly, from what I could see and observe and assess, they were more looters than anything else, these groups. And they were removed. The Crisis Staff, while we had the Territorial Defence and especially later, after the setting up of the VRS, they were eliminated, they were thrown out. They were told in no uncertain terms that they are undesirable in Foca and that they had to leave, and they left our area. They were active for a brief time, maybe in April, until the end of April, from the 8th of April until the end of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you said, "especially later after the setting up of the VRS, they were eliminated." Did anyone come from outside Foca to resolve the paramilitary problem?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: There was a constant conflict going on between them and the Territorial Defence and the Crisis Staff, but finally and formally that was resolved after June. Ratko Mladic also came to Foca and he put things in order, completely the way it should be and the way the army, the future army of our Republika Srpska should actually comport themselves. As far as I can recall, it was either July or late June when Ratko Mladic arrived in Foca for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question to clarify? You said they were looters and they were thrown out. But were they not investigated and arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, some were arrested and brought in, but there was no particular investigation, in fact. Many of them just left, left in an unknown direction, probably left to wherever it was that they had come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us the names of some who were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I really do not know a single one. I just know -- I could recognise the faces of some and I do not know their first names or their last names or to what groups they belonged or what the name of the group was. I don't know that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And those arrested, what was done with them? Were they investigated? Were they prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that they were detained because that would have caused huge conflict between the paramilitary forces and our Territorial Defence prior to the establishment of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to now call up document 1D04145 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with this publication that's on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I'm familiar with it. This is the paper called Vox, which quite a long time before the war broke out was published by the Muslims, and Senad Pasic, nicknamed Saja, was actually the main protagonist of that. I had it several times before in front of me. It was a bi-weekly or a monthly; it is not a daily. But it was published. It came out for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The individual that you identified as the protagonist of the paper, Senad Pasic, nicknamed Saja, did he have links to any political party?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He was the president of the SDA, local chapter, the municipal organisation, and he cooperated closely with Alija Izetbegovic, with Cengic, with Halid Cengic from Odzaci, from Ustikolina, et cetera. He was a grocer. Actually, he had a shop. He traded in agricultural produce, fruit, vegetables and such like.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was this publication distributed and read in Foca during 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I did not buy it, and I did not hear about its being sold, but it was distributed. I had it before me, several issues in fact, on several occasions. This paper had very vitriolic and dangerous messages, vis-à-vis the Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 2 of the document in both languages, there is an Article entitled, "What to do with Serbs in the Islamic Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Are you familiar with this article?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I've read it several times, and to tell you honestly, I do not remember all the details after so much time. But this article sends the message how the Serbs could remain in Bosnia and Herzegovina, how they should comport themselves, what lay in store for them. This is something that when you read it, it really raises the hairs on your head and you get goose bumps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What was the reaction of both Serbs and Muslims in Foca to this article when it came out?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: There were many Muslims too who were dissatisfied with what was being written, with the fact that something of this kind was being written, because there were good neighbourly relations and the connections, many Muslims and many Serbs did not wish for this to happen in Bosnia-Herzegovina or for any kind of war to be provoked. It was quite clear to both Serbs and Muslims. The Muslims protested, they aired their grievances, and the Serbs were very much afraid. They were dreading because of what was in store for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D4145 receives number D580, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D580 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, for my last topic, if we could turn back to D579, your written statement, and page 3 in both languages, focusing on paragraph 12. Now, sir, in paragraph 12 you state that, "During April clashes in Foca, Muslim places of worship, mosques, from where Muslims opened fire and engaged us were destroyed or damaged." I want to know, when and in what manner were these mosques destroyed or damaged, as you state in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I have to elaborate a bit on this particular question, if you will allow me. Namely the Muslims started to arm themselves quite early on, which they did through Focatrans. Perhaps the Foca conflict, the Focatrans conflict between the Serbs and Muslim workers there is known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, that appears already in your statement. There is no need to repeat what is already in your statement. So would you please focus your answer on what Mr. Ivetic specifically asked you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So when the Muslims procured arms and imported weapons into Foca, they predominantly put them in some places of worship. Some, not all. This is where they stored their weapons, the explosive substances and such like. Furthermore, in parallel, in some of those facilities, such as the Pilav mosque in Gornje Polje, they trained the Green Berets and their armed forces and the Patriotic League. There were quite a few people who came from elsewhere, from other parts, from the Sandzak, for instance, and with the war -- I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I didn't see you. I can stop immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because you're now explaining to us what activities took place in those mosques, but the question was when and in what manner the mosques were destroyed or damaged. That was the question. Could you please focus on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These mosques were demolished, for the most part, in conflicts, in combat activities, precisely because the Muslims opened fire from the minarets of some of these mosques. I personally could see Muslims shelling Serb positions and Serb houses from some mosques. And then on the other hand, later, sometime in 1995, after the NATO forces fired several projectiles on Foca, these mosques, as very old buildings, were damaged considerably and demolished. This is how these places of worship came to be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And can you then tell us perhaps a bit more detail. Were they shelled or was it other arms that were used that caused the damage or the destruction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in 1995, there was in the immediate vicinity around the bridges, the upper and lower Drina bridge where these NATO shells impacted, that's where the places of worship were, these old buildings, dilapidated buildings, 300 or 400 years old, that is one thing. And during the conflict, on the other hand, between the Serbs and the Muslims, these facilities, one of these --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: -- was demolished because the recoilless gun was the heaviest piece of weaponry that the Territorial Defence had, and its shell could, if it fell on a mosque, it could destroy it. But it was only used against facilities where there were Muslim forces opening fire against Serb houses and Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You distinguished between the damage done during combat in, I understand, the early stages of the conflict, and you told us about NATO shelling. Did NATO shells hit mosques or was it -- or were they damaged by NATO shells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Not a single projectile fell on the mosques, but they did fall in the vicinity of the mosques. Some mosques were nearer; some were farther. The nearer ones were damaged. I know that when the shells landed on the bridges and around the bridges and on some other facilities, my flat also was completely devastated. All the glass panes were shattered. The door jambs were actually dislodged. And this was the kind of fire that was opened. So we were also collateral damage, and that was collateral damage generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's focus on the mosques. Could you tell us which -- first of all, did you personally observe the shelling by NATO that damaged mosques?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I personally did see. For instance, the mosque near --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what impact was closest to a mosque so as to damage it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around 100 or 150 metres, in that circle there were several mosques which are in the town of Foca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us on what those shells or the closest shell impacted? Was that an open space? Was that a street? Was that a house? Was that a military facility? Could you tell us on what the closest shell, as you said, 100 or 150 metres away from the mosque, on what it exactly impacted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They hit the bridges on the Drina and the repeater on the Kumur. That's a military installation of the former Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in this same paragraph of your statement, paragraph 12, you talk of your personal observations at the Pilav mosque and what you saw there. What I want to know is what year was this? Was it before or after the war started?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: At the Pilav mosque in Gornje Polje, training went on of the Green Berets. That was considerably before the war broke out in Foca. That was in March and in February 1992. I personally went into this mosque later to see, because I was interested because a man worked with me who was called Pilav, the Pilav mosque, and when he told me what had had happened in the Pilav mosque, he told me it has fallen upon this generation to reconstruct this mosque. But it was not reconstruction, it was actually training, because there was a blackboard in this mosque and I don't see that a blackboard is used for prayers to Allah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir, for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that ends the examination. I see we are also at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is time for the break. We will take a break of 20 minutes, Mr. Vujicic. After the break, you'll be cross-examined. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, before we start, three hours were announced. Is that what you really need?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I expect to come in substantially under that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vujicic, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Bibles, you'll find her to your right. Ms. Bibles is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like to start by asking some background questions, but I think I'll preface my questioning by commenting or asking you to do a favour. You've testified that you were a jurist during your career so you would understand the importance of listening carefully to the question and then, please, only answering the question that I've asked. Can you agree to do that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I shall refrain as much as I can. I understand. You are right in what you're saying. That's very important. That is simultaneous interpretation. One has to understand the question and respond only then.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, you've testified that Foca was a large -- the largest municipality in Bosnia. I want to just go over a few features of Foca. First, is it true that it bordered with Montenegro to the south?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And Gorazde, which was a Muslim enclave during the war, is on the northeastern border of Foca municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: From Foca, downstream about 30 kilometres. That is how far away the town of Gorazde is from the town of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And the Drina River flows right through the middle of Foca town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Not through the centre. Foca is on the right bank of the Drina, more than 90 per cent of it, and the Drina flows to Gorazde on the left, but then through Gorazde it basically goes through the centre of town. So Gorazde is both on the left and right banks of the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree that the area known as the Sarajevo municipalities shared a border with the north central part of Foca?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Foca had a border with the western part of the municipality of Gacko, then Nevesinje, and to the east Trnovo. Partly in the local commune of Jabuka, there was the area of Jahorina and there was the border with the municipality of Pale there, and then what I've already said, Gorazde. And what I've already said, Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, even in my wildest imagination, I could not think of any dispute about these geographical matters. Now, if you need them for the witness, then just put it to him and ask your questions. But we have now spent a couple of minutes just on the layout of the municipalities, et cetera, which is really superfluous, I would say. We have maps, by the way. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree that all of these locations, the Drina, the various Sarajevo municipalities, and the Montenegrin border, were all important locations or points for the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection; calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, if you could first explore what the witness knows about the positions taken by the Bosnian Serb leadership, then we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honours I'll return to this. I'll move on from this point and come back to it a little bit later.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree that in 1991, a slight majority of the residents in Foca were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: This is what I can say to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, moving on, you were mobilised on or about the 26th of April 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What was that, the 26th of April?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Is it true that you were mobilised on or about the 26th of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Exactly on the 26th of April. That was the first day of my mobilisation. That was the 26th of April. It was Easter.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that you remained in the military until 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, until June 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, what can I say? They changed. They --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, let's start, then, who was your commander when you were initially mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: It was Zoran Vukovic, commander of the 1st Battalion, and I was mobilised into that battalion as a soldier, a marksman in the trenches.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, when you testified today at transcript page 11, temporary transcript page 11, line 24, there may have been a mistake when you discussed the 11th and 12th Foca Light Infantry Brigade. What were the correct numbers for the brigades from Foca?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, the 11th and 12th Light Infantry Brigade of Foca, two brigades. They were established only after the month of June. Say up until the 15th of July, and until that time, there was the Territorial Defence and there was the Crisis Staff that was in charge of this Territorial Defence. There were combatants from villages who defended their villages, and they all grouped together and that's how the Territorial Defence was established. And it operated, say, up until the 15th of July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, which of the Foca Light Infantry Brigades were you a part of?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: The 1st Battalion of the Light Infantry Brigade, the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And just to be clear, is it true that the order incorporating the Serb forces of Foca into the VRS was by order dated 29 June 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I just know that up until that time, there was the Territorial Defence, and there was the order of Marko Kovac of this tactical group to establish units of the Army of Republika Srpska up until the 5th or 6th or 15th of July --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: -- that year, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could see P2838 on our screens?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, as this document comes up, I'd first like you to just take a look at the document and then I will have a question for you. Sir, is this the order by Kovac that you were just describing?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is an order of the commander of the tactical group, Marko Kovac. This was the very beginning, and then from that moment onwards, the territorial units were supposed to grow into the Army of Republika Srpska. I don't remember these deadlines very well. It's been a long time. But I remember full well that it was Marko Kovac's order. It was the end of June, the 29th of June, on the basis of an order of a higher command. This was issued --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The date 29th June, has that been refreshed, then, by looking at this document?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: This is correct, the 29th of June. That's when the order was issued. And as for the --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: There was this deadline up until when the units of the VRS were supposed to be established in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, again, I'll remind you, if you can listen very closely to the question I'm asking and simply answer the question. I'm next going to shift gears a little bit and talk about or ask you about some of the commanders of the Bosnian Serb units in Foca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you do that, can I ask a question?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, you've been talking about the 11th and the 12th Light Infantry Brigade. I see this order refers to the 1st Foca Light Infantry Brigade. Could there be a mistake somewhere? Or did you belong to the 1st Light Infantry Brigade and not the 12th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To tell you the truth, when I was mobilised -- well, maybe afterwards it was the 11th and the 12th. Maybe it was just the Light Infantry Brigade of Foca. I don't remember very well. I was not really in these military commands. I was a rifleman at the separation line, this administration line between Gorazde and Foca, Zebina Suma. That's what this area is called and I stayed there all the way up until 1994. Maybe it was just this one Light Infantry Brigade and then later on two were formed out of that one, the 11th and the 12th. But all of this was up until the end of June. After the month of June, as I've already said, the Army of Republika Srpska was established and this went on all the way up until mid-July that year.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could turn to the second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And sir, at the top of the page, you'll see that this order distinguishes which battalions are in the 1st Foca Light Infantry Brigade and which are in the 2nd Foca Light Infantry Brigade. Now, looking at this, it appears that you would have been in the 2nd Foca Light Infantry Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the B/C/S it's not on the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: About halfway down the page, sir, do you see the division of the two brigades?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I don't know when this Territorial Defence was divided up into these brigades but at the time when I was mobilised, I was mobilised into the 1st Battalion. I think it was the 12th Light Infantry Brigade. That's what it was called then. Later on, these brigades were abolished and they all became one brigade in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to ask a question. You seem to have trouble remembering some of the details from back then. Is that -- is that a difficulty for you in remembering details from 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, some details. Well, at my age, 22 years later, it's possible that I don't remember some details. But what is important is the question. And then if I remember later, I will tell you. But if I simply cannot remember, then I'm going to tell you that too, that I simply cannot state anything because I don't remember. So that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to shift topics and I'd like to ask you what you know or what you remember about some of the commanders of the Bosnian Serb units in Foca. First, Brane Kosevic led an intervention unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: This is the first time that I hear this name, now, from you. I really cannot say anything because I have never heard of this name before.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: How about Gojko Jankovic? Was he a commander that you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I remember Gojko Jankovic, not Jerkovic. You know what? I've already said that this Territorial Defence consisted of Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Village guards.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Jankovic was somewhere from Brod, near Suceska. He was not the commander. He was, I mean, the commander of some reconnaissance unit, the so-called intervention unit which later on, when Foca calmed down, when there were no problems, when there were no clashes, then the war continued in the villages. And then Gojko was out in the field and he was observing how and where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The simple question was whether you were familiar with that name, and Ms. Bibles will then put further --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, correct. I do know the name, yes, Gojko Jankovic. I know Gojko Jankovic. Yes, Gojko Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wait for the next question, what Ms. Bibles would like to further ask you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you know who he reported to?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: There was the tactical group or rather the Crisis Staff, and it was in charge of the Territorial Defence. To tell you the truth, the Crisis Staff, as far as individuals are concerned, I really don't know. Very often they would not have one particular officer in charge, especially in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: It was a question of saving Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, if you could try to focus your answers on the very specific questions that I've asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, in all fairness to the witness, if you ask to whom he was reporting, then the witness may not know whether you intended to say what entity or what person, and he explained that. So to that extent, I would think that he focused on your question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to Pero Elez. Which battalion was he the commander for?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was battalion commander for a while, but I know that he was a commander of a group in the area of Miljevina. Pero Elez from Miljevina, I knew had him personally. He was killed during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like to shift gears now and talk a little bit about your political role, both before and then after the war. Is it true that you lived in the largest local commune in Foca?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's true. The local commune of Gornje Polje, I had two terms of office as president of that local commune and then the war started during my second term of office.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like to ask just a couple of questions about that. Before the war, first, were you a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. But before the war, or actually just before the conflict broke out, I was a member of the SDS. I became a member then, but I was not part of any of the SDS organs, the municipal organisation of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So, sir, your position as president of the local commune before the war was a purely municipal function as opposed to the SDS position?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, the local commune, according to the constitution that was in force then, was a territorial organisation. It was called a local commune, it had certain functions within the civilian authorities, and everything that happened happened in cooperation with the municipal organs and the municipal administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: It resolved the problems of the citizens in that area. It had its statute, it had its organs, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In that vein, if we could bring 65 ter 08611 to our screens, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, this is the Official Gazette of the Serbian Municipality of Foca. If we could start at page 1 in both languages. Starting at the page that's on our screen, we read, "First session of the Assembly of the Serbian municipality of Foca," and, "pursuant to the decision to establish the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina of 25 December 1991," and then after some legal language, it notes, "the decision to establish the Assembly of the Serbian People in Foca municipality." Is this -- what we are looking at here, is that what you were just describing in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: No. I was not an assemblyman. I did not work in the administration of the municipality or in the executive organs or in the assembly of the municipality. I had no function there whatsoever. The session where this was promulgated, all of that had nothing to do with me. And to tell you the truth, I know that this was promulgated, but this is the first time that I see this decision before me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 3 in the English at Article 6 but stay on page 1 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If I could have you look at Article 6, sir, we see, "The assembly of Serbian people in Foca municipality shall recognise the validity of all federal regulations." Does this mean regulations, sir, from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since the Municipal Assembly was established in the beginning of the war actually, I wanted to say that there weren't any regulations in force. So everything that existed in the days of the former Yugoslavia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in terms of republican regulations and federal regulations, it says here that all of that should be taken over and that all of this will be acknowledged until new regulations are passed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, if we could move to the top of page 4 in the English and the middle of the second column in page 1 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We see the date for this entry is 25 December 1991. Now, sir, the Chamber has received evidence that just a few days before this, the main board of the SDS issued instructions that Serb assemblies should be created. Were you aware of those instructions?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: No. No. Really. I did not know about that. I did not have those instructions before me. I never saw that. I really don't know. I didn't even go into that kind of thing. It was the beginning of the war. There was a lot of commotion, a lot of nervousness. So many things and all sorts of things. And I didn't really go into any of that. As a matter of fact I thought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you said you didn't know. That's the answer to the question. Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could go to page 14 in the English, and unfortunately, I am not sure where to go in the B/C/S. I believe it's the second page. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Third page, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, you did talk about the Statute of the -- I believe the Serb municipality of Foca. Were you present at the Assembly of the Serbian People in Foca on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's zoomed in on the wrong part of the page. The Statute seems to be a little bit higher up on the right-hand side. Could we just check that --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- where it reads, "Statute." Right side of the page, approximately the middle, that's where I see in Cyrillic, "Statute." Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: All right. Sir, were you present at the assembly on the 3rd of April 1992, when this was officially promulgated?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, I was not an assemblyman. I was not -- I had no relevance to the municipality. I was talking about the Statute of the local commune, not the Statute of the municipality. So nobody invited me to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you were present in whatever capacity. Were you present or were you not present when this was promulgated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was not present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That answers the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, before we leave this page, I'll note that the new municipality was part of the Serb Autonomous Region of Herzegovina. This was the political entity the Serbs had declared the previous fall, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I cannot say anything about that, really. It was not something that I was concerned with much actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But were you aware that there was a Serb Autonomous Region of Herzegovina been declared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do I know? I cannot answer that, really, because I'm not familiar with that thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But did you know that it existed at all or were you unaware of the establishment of such a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew that the municipality of Foca, that there had been an Assembly of the Serbian People in Foca, that this statute was adopted. But I didn't participate and how it all unfolded I cannot say anything about that, whether it was part of eastern Herzegovina. But I know that it is territorially linked with eastern Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That, again, was not my question. I mean, you said you were a lawyer. Were you aware of the establishment of something that was called the Serb Autonomous Region of Herzegovina? Did you read it? Did you hear it? Did you know about it in any other way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't know, then that has answered the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not know about it, nor had I read about it. I was at the front-line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's the position of the Prosecution that it was established in fall 1991. So, therefore, you were not at the front-line at that time, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not at the front-line, but neither was I in any of the municipal bodies and I did not have anything to do with the preparation or the adoption of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the witness said he wasn't aware of it. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask that the gazette be MFIed. I'll discuss with Defence counsel whether we can reach an agreement as to whether certain portions of the contents should be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 8611 receives number P6680, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6680 is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, sir, you have previously testified in the Karadzic case on the 17th of January 2013. Do you recall testifying in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I do. That was last year, in January.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you. And, sir, you have signed two witness statements for this Tribunal. Is it accurate that one was for the Karadzic case, for the Karadzic Defence, and one was for the Mladic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I signed one for the Defence -- for the Mladic Defence recently and previously I had signed one for the Karadzic Defence. And when I signed for the Defences of Karadzic and Mladic, I stated that I would say what I knew, whether it was in my favour or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The simple question was whether you gave those two statements. The answer apparently is yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Let us go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree with me that your statement in the Karadzic case is 33 paragraphs long? Would you have any reason to dispute that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I know that I gave the statement. I do not recall exactly how long it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, today, for reference, at temporary transcript page 15, starting at line 22, you testified that Ratko Mladic came to Foca in June of 1992. Would you agree with me that this information is not in your Mladic statement, in your Karadzic statement, or in your Karadzic testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, I didn't say that in the Karadzic case. But as regards June, I cannot tell you with precision whether he came in June or July. But he did come to Foca around the time the VRS was constituted and organised, and that was at the end of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The gist of the question was whether you ever mentioned this before, either in the statement or in your testimony, and that is today for the first time that you referred to that visit. And I do understand your answer to be that you confirm that it's the first time, today, that you mention it. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I didn't say so in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you mention or did you talk about this visit of Mladic to Foca during any of your meetings with the Mladic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I did not see Mladic with my own eyes. I only know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I immediately stop you again. The question was whether, in your conversations with the Mladic Defence, whether you had mentioned this visit of Mr. Mladic to Foca in June, at whatever date. Did you mention that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which Defence of Mladic's? I do not know that man at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. You were interviewed by members of the Mladic Defence team, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In March of this year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I know that -- generally know that Ratko Mladic once came to Foca in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, you're not answering the questions. The question is: During the interview which, as we see on the record, was conducted in March of this year, did you mention to those who interviewed you the visit of Mr. Mladic? Did you mention that during that interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To tell you frankly, I do not remember. I might have mentioned it, if I had been asked about it or had had I been asked about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 30981 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, this is the statement that you gave to the Karadzic Defence. I'd like ask you some questions about some issues which you address in your Karadzic statement which have not been included in your Mladic statement. If we could go to paragraph 3, when this comes up. Sir, in paragraph 3, you describe the Serbian Democratic Party holding a rally in Foca in September 1991 attended by representatives of the Serbian parties from other municipalities. Do you recall this information? Just "yes" or "no".

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I do recall it, yes. It was in September and present were --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Later in the same paragraph, you say that that year, which we understand to be 1991: "Both national parties started their own preparations to protect the people. The SDA prepared the Muslims and the Serbian side prepared the Serbs. This involved obtaining weapons for the people through secret channels, but I do not know exactly where and how." Simply, do you stand by this evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot stand by these words exactly to the effect that the Serbian Democratic Party was preparing the Serbian people for something like that. But I do know well what the situation was like when it came to the illegal arming, especially of Muslims in the city of Foca, and how that unfolded. When they saw that, the Serbs started arming themselves a bit later, and procuring weapons in different ways. This is what I can say.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So, sir, just to make sure I understand the answer, and that is that you do not at this point stand by your evidence as presented in the Karadzic statement as to that point?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I do stand in respect of the Serbian Democratic Party, namely that they started doing so later. But for a while, when it comes to the preparation for war, it was rather passive, the SDS was rather passive relative to the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to move now to paragraph 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, unless you would leave that for a later stage, I would need an explanation for the witness about the change. But if you deal with it at a later stage, I'll refrain from asking any questions at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we should stay on page -- this may be a good time to address that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say it's better not at this moment. I'll let you proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, obviously, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you deal with the matter in the way you have planned, then I'm happy, but it's not something that we should ignore.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, in paragraph 18, you say, "I also know that the JNA, which had smaller units guarding military facilities in the Foca area, completely pulled out from Foca in May 1992." Do you stand by this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Not in May, and before -- in March, and before March, it is then that they started to withdraw. They had their depots, their warehouses, and they were evacuating them and taking materiel away. And this was a long time ago -- a long time before the war broke out in Foca. So these depots were evacuated. These military facilities were in Ustikolina and Gorazde and they were under Muslim control. So it was not in May. This army did not exist. There was no army in Foca at all. We only had the Territorial Defence then, not the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, so just to make sure that I'm clear, this information in paragraph 18, where you describe the JNA pulling out from Foca in May of 1992, is it your testimony today that you no longer stand by that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: The way it is written here, I said that the Yugoslav army withdrew from Bosnia-Herzegovina sometime in May, but not from Foca. There was no Yugoslav army in Foca at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, if we could move on now to paragraph 20, in paragraph 20, you say: "I do not know who took what from the JNA facilities, and I cannot say much about that. All I know is that the depots found by the armed forces of Republika Srpska after the withdrawal of the JNA became property of the Serbian armed units. A large part of the equipment, heavy weapons and the like, were subsequently taken by the JNA units with them. The weapons which the Serbian forces seized in these depots were mainly infantry weapons. I know that the Muslim forces locked the depot at Ustikolina and took from the depot shelves anti-tank mines and the like, weapons which killed most Serbian soldiers. The military depots were held --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you move to the next page --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Oh, yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct, what you've said.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: "The military depots were held by the Muslim forces until mid-May." Do you stand by this evidence today?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: They left a bit before that, because that was sometime in late April, towards the end of April, that the Muslim forces, which held the military depots in Ustikolina left. But these depots were totally empty. They were empty, first of all, because the Yugoslav army had long ago, in February that year, carted away everything of interest, and the rest which remained was distributed by the Muslim forces to their fighters so that when we entered those depots they were completely empty.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, in mid-May or, if I'm understanding your testimony today, perhaps earlier than that, is it correct, then, that the military depots were taken by the Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: The Serb forces entered those depots, and the one in Ustikolina, three days after Easter. I was in that unit so I know well that they entered Ustikolina on the 28th or the 29th. I'm not sure. It might be a couple of days. But I do know that there was absolutely nothing in those depots. These were completely empty hangars.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, was one of the military depots in - I'm going to spell it - Livade, L-i-v-a-d-e?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: No. At Livade was the Territorial Defence and they had infantry weapons for the training of the Territorial Defence there. In those depots, when the war flared up, those depots were entered by the Serb forces of the Territorial Defence and the Muslim forces entered the penitentiary, the KP Dom, and there were infantry weapons on both sides. And the Muslim forces also entered Focatrans, and these weapons were predominantly for training purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, moving on to a different topic within your statement in the Karadzic case, if we could move to paragraph 16, you also described non-Serbs leaving Foca. In this paragraph you say: "The Muslim inhabitants from the town --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we wait for a second so we can have the relevant portion enlarged for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You also describe non-Serbs leaving Foca in this paragraph. Here you say: "The Muslim inhabitants from the town started leaving Foca, going to other locations outside Foca and Bosnia-Herzegovina, Montenegro, Serbia, the Dubrovnik area, the Adriatic coast, and Macedonia." So can you confirm that you know Muslims fled from Foca across the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina into other countries?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that that happened. Some left before the conflict, and most of them withdrew together with the Green Berets and the Patriotic League. But at the same time, Serb civilians also left, and many buildings in Foca town remained deserted. In my own building, there were 40 flats and only I remained and another person. Everybody else had left.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, I --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: On a temporary basis, albeit.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, I just want you to confirm that you know that Muslims led -- fled from Foca across the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina into other countries.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that they fled. They left because of the war. Just like Serbs left Foca for a while. I can give you some details, if you would like me to, how these matters unfolded. I had a friend who called me, he said, "My house is damaged. I'm leaving, if you can look after my house."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered the question that you do confirm that they left and I do understand that, that they left across the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina into other countries. Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Some of them left and some remained in Foca, and they stated that they were leaving Foca in order to reunite with their families. That is what I stand by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but at the same time, what Ms. Bibles read to you is that they went to other countries through Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you say that they reunited with their families in other countries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. But nobody actually expelled them from Foca. Some of them remained throughout the summer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That wasn't the question. But since you're insisting so much on it, how many stayed after all in Foca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A great many remained in Foca, and some of them remained throughout the war. They didn't go anywhere. Some were in units of the VRS, Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the exact percentage but a large number certainly remained. After the Green Berets -- when the Green Berets were leaving Foca and after that, many civilians remained and some families left occasionally after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said that you don't know the exact percentage. Was it more than 10?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More than 10 per cent. Over 10 per cent. Perhaps approximately 50 per cent remained in Foca town, and some left towards Gorazde with Green Beret units. Where to, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber also heard evidence that after the initial conflict, that Foca was 99 per cent Serb. That's not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The Serbs also left at that time, and they returned after a certain period. But there were, in terms of percentages, there were by far more Muslims in Foca. I know that well. Other people can interpret it differently but I know that for a fact. There were many more Muslims and many more than 10 per cent, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. After the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Proceed, Ms. Bibles. I said please proceed but it's time for a break. Witness, if you would follow the usher, we would take a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 10 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We left off, sir, with paragraph 16 of your statement in Karadzic. You continued on to say, referring to the Muslims: "They asked to leave and for their relocation to be provided. They requested buses free of charge and the buses were provided to them. I was present when they asked for temporary relocation. Everything they asked for was provided to them, and they were also told that no one was forcing them to do this but they voluntarily decided to do it." Sir, the request that you're discussing, this was made to the war commission; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: It was made to some organs there. This was practically around the Municipal Assembly, the Executive Board of the assembly. I remember very well that I was present on one occasion when that happened and I know that that's the way it was in general. What you read out is correct. I have nothing else to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, the war commission's June 1992 decision on this point is P2822.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
