utterances.text: Sir, you then go on to say: "That was the situation in Foca municipality in 1992, after which, due to such fierce interethnic clashes, Foca became practically a complete Serbian area." Now, do you stand by this statement, that Foca became practically a complete Serbian area in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: When we are talking about the authorities, it was the Serb authorities, purely Serb. But there were Serbs, Muslims and Montenegrins living there throughout the war. The population was mixed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, just to make sure that I -- that we understand this, are you saying that you do stand by your statement but that it doesn't read the way it appears to read, or are you saying that you do not stand by your statement that Foca became practically a complete Serbian area in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, I think, in fairness -- excuse me, sir. I think in fairness to the witness, the statement does say that also if you read on in that same paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, to go on to finish the paragraph, you state: "I cannot say that it remained a Serbian area because the Muslim inhabitants had been expelled because no one forced them to leave. There were those Muslims who safely remained in Foca for the duration of the clashes while others fought in the units of the Army of Republika Srpska. I know of at least ten of them." Now, sir, trying to make sense of this, is the issue that you had in this paragraph the notion that Muslims had been expelled or was it the -- or was it a Serb municipality in 1992, a mostly Serb municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, to say that they were expelled, that is mind-boggling, that I would say something like that, that I would accept something like that? No way. They left of their own free will. But then as far as the authorities in the municipality, during the war, the authorities were Serb but the population was Serb, Croatian, Montenegrin, Muslim, certain percentages; other ethnic groups as well. That is what I can say. And that is what I would accept as a statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree that you didn't mention the departure of Muslims at any point in your Mladic statement?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: What, in the statement? I'm sorry, I didn't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, actually we'll move on to the conditions that the Muslims lived in in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For the record, paragraph 8 of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: That's where I was directing, to paragraph 8, if we could go to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Lukic, I think paragraph 8 says the women left the facility, not necessarily left Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the third sentence, "The Muslims began to leave Foca."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In paragraph 8 of the statement, let's go through this, you describe measures that civilian authorities took to protect the Muslims in Foca. You say first they brought Muslims from distant villages where they could not be "controlled and protected to certain facilities in Foca where they could be defended." Do you affirm today that Muslims from the villages in Foca municipality were brought to Foca town and brought to certain facilities where they would be kept under guard?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: A small part of the rural Muslim population in the municipality of Foca withdrew with the armed Green Berets and the Patriotic League, whereas some people, especially women, frail old men, et cetera, stayed at home. In order to protect that population, it was suggested or, rather, the civilian and military authorities decided to take care of their safety so that nothing undesirable would happen to that population. That was it. Some centres were organised, like Partizan for women and so on. So they came to Foca, and they saw Serb families, Muslim families, who lived there, I mean this rural population. A large portion of the population left on time and then some people just stayed at home, either here or there, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: When you say a large portion of the population left on time, what is the time you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: At the time of the conflict and before the conflict, that's when they withdrew. On both sides, there were -- there was fear, Serbs and Muslims. My village, Vrbnica, on the slopes of Zelengora, a lot of people left and the Muslim units took it without any resistance whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, going on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, could I ask one question? In this statement given to the Karadzic Defence, you explained in more detail than you did in the statement given to the Mladic Defence about how the women were brought to the Partizan sports hall. You also said the inhabitants of those villages who said they wanted to stay in their homes were enabled to do so. Could you tell us how many stayed in their homes despite the security offered to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In some houses, in certain villages, there were some old men and also there were women there throughout the war, and then later on they would link up with their own family members at some point in time, which percentage and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many approximately stayed in those villages where they were offered security. That these were men and women, I do understand. But could you tell us in a bit more detail how many finally stayed in their houses and did not follow the invitation to come to the Partizan sports hall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know what? You know what? I've already explained that the municipality of Foca is very big, with scattered villages, et cetera. After the Green Berets left and the civilian population with them and before them, so here and there, in some houses, there were some civilians left. And there were some people who expressed their wish not to leave their homes and they stayed in those houses then. As for others --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop you there? Did you go to those houses, to those villages, and were you present when people were left the choice either to stay or to follow to the Partizan sports hall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in some places and I was not in others. Where my unit went, that's where I was. That's where I was present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that this happened during the first stages of the conflict when you were not yet in a unit. As you said, you stood guard at the place where the women and children were kept. At that time, did you go to the villages --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not go to the village and I don't know about that. I lived in town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you don't have firsthand knowledge of what was told to those who were invited to come to the Partizan sports hall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can just say here what it was that I heard. But that I was on the spot before I was engaged, I cannot say anything. I cannot say this; I cannot say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Going back to paragraph 8, you described that the second measure the civilian authorities took to protect Muslims in Foca is by mopping up the whole area of Foca municipality from Islamic soldiers and their formations. Is it true that Foca municipality was completely mopped up by the end of April?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: No, no. Some areas had not been cleansed. There were Muslim forces there keeping them under their control, like the local commune of Suceska, Jelec, and so on. Suceska, all the way up until the month of October, there were negotiations between them, to take care of things so that no one would attack anyone, that there should be no incursions in those villages and so on. To tell you the truth, as far as Suceska was concerned, this was violated by the Muslim side. So my village, which belonged to Suceska, was razed to the ground, totally empty. In the month of April, people moved out and it was only in the month of August, the 8th of August, that it was devastated.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, moving on to paragraph 33 of your Karadzic statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I nevertheless ask a question? Do I understand you well that part of the Foca municipality remained under Muslim control whereas other parts were under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the part that was under --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean those areas up there, those rural areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the parts that were under Serb control, were they completely mopped up by the end of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up until the end of April, as far as the armed forces are concerned, the situation was quite clear. All of that had been cleansed, and as I've already said, quite a few civilians had stayed behind. The idea was to get rid of the Green Berets, who were breaking into Serbian villages and committing crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how did you know exactly if you would see a male person not in uniform whether he would be a Green Beret or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Green Berets were marked. Marked. They had these caps. They had had these insignia on their own, on the epaulettes of their coats and so on. That was afterwards. But while they were preparing in secret, then they acted as if they were the civilian population. There were some in my very own building in town too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, during this mopping up, was every male -- well, let's say, between 18 and 55, recognisable as a Green Beret, or were there also normal male civilians not identified as Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite a few Muslims were not among the Green Berets. They didn't want to join any armed units. These people were loyal who did not want war, and people like that stayed on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you tell us what approximately the portion of those was among the Muslim population? Was it one-third? Was it a half? Was it 10 per cent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you that at first, the Green Berets and the Patriotic League were mostly people from elsewhere, and to a lesser extent, ethnic Muslims from Foca. Later on, the war was raging and there was general mobilisation on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not an answer to my question. My question was, and I'll further specify it: What, approximately, was the percentage of the male local population that was identified as Green Berets or Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everybody on the ground was recognised, those who were local citizens who didn't want to join the Green Berets or the Patriotic League, and the Green Berets were recognisable. The civilians who did not join the Green Berets, well, that was a lesser number in the villages, on the ground. To tell you the truth, I cannot tell you which percentage exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to go to paragraph 33 of your Karadzic statement. Continuing the discussion about Muslims who were accommodated in Foca town, in paragraph 33, you mention that Muslims from neighbouring villages were accommodated, and you testified about this in Karadzic. Would you stand by the proposition that they came from villages, these Muslims, where there had been conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: The civilian population that stayed behind was accepted. They were received at the reception centres. That's the way it was. And I stand by that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You stand by that the civilians who were in Foca town were civilians who had come from villages in Foca where there had been conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can counsel direct where that is in paragraph 33 of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could go to the Karadzic transcript, 32097, and I'll have to get the 65 ter number for that. I believe it's 30980.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, what will now be read to you is not available in your own language so carefully listen to what Ms. Bibles reads to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked: "Q. Did I understand you properly? Were those Muslims from the villages that were affected by conflict?" Your answer: "A. Yes, precisely. Those people came from villages that were some 15 -- excuse me, 10 to 15 kilometres away from Foca. Neither Serbian forces nor the police could guarantee their safety. They could not promise them that they wouldn't go unscathed. When the Muslim armed forces left those villages, they remained unprotected and those of the people who were left behind were women and elderly. Men would be accommodated in some other facilities where they were protected, for example they were accommodated in the penal institute, there were Serbs and Muslims there, and they were some of the convicts who had been tried before the war, whereas the female population was accommodated in some facilities where there was room as a rule." I believe I'll leave it there. Do you stand by that testimony in the Karadzic case, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Entirely, entirely.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And now I was going to go back to paragraph 33 of the statement, unless there were questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one question. Those men that would be accommodated in other facilities such as the penal institute, were they treated in a different way compared to those who were detained there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for this male population that had been accommodated at the KP Dom Foca, I cannot really say much about them. But I know full well, as far as food is concerned, that all the convicts and all the officials working there got their food from the very same pots. It was as if these people were at home. If they wanted to, they could leave, as far as the male population was concerned. This was mainly old people, old men. That was the structure. The structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They could walk in and out the KP Dom, which was a penitentiary institution, at their free will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were treated somewhat differently compared to the convicts from before the war. They had the right to communicate. I don't know whether they had the right to go out. I was not there and I cannot tell you for sure. I can just tell you about what my brother said. He worked there. He had an office job there, and I can tell you what the situation was like based on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to take you back to your previous answer where you said, if they wanted to, they could leave, as far as the male population was concerned. Now, in answer to my next question, you say, I do not know whether they would leave at free will. Yes or no? Do I take that the last answer is the one I can rely upon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant actually I understand your question whether they could occasionally leave and go to town. But when it came to leaving Foca, they had the same right as those who lived in the houses, those Muslims who lived in their houses, just as they could decide whether they wanted to stay or go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My simple question was: Could they leave the detention facility as they wished to do whatever they wanted to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the city or outside the city?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, irrespective.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. I cannot say. All I can say is that they had the right to opt for leaving Foca. As regards their getting out of the facility and going into town, I don't know about that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which would actually mean that if they did not choose to leave Foca municipality, that they were deprived of their liberty to enter and leave the facility where they were kept, as you said, in order to secure their safety.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were entitled to a decision, whether they would go back to their homes, stay with friends in town, or move out of Foca. They had that right. They were not actually shut up there. They were received there. That's a great difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One earlier answer was that you didn't know, but apparently you now do know. Ms. Bibles, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, this Trial Chamber has heard and considered evidence that the men who were detained in KP Dom were in fact not free to leave the facility. I put it to you that your evidence today on that point is either in error or that you just don't know and you're making it up.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: No. Perhaps I'm not understood. Maybe I'm not quite clear but I shall repeat. When it came to whether they went out during the day, whether they had the right to leave the KP Dom and go back to it during the day, that is something I cannot say. But what I can say is that these people, these elderly men, who were there staying there, accommodated there had on a temporary basis, they could apply to the civilian authorities just like any other citizen and apply for either leaving the town of Foca or returning to their holdings, to their homes. I hope I was sufficiently clear now. I don't know how else to explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What Ms. Bibles put to you is that this is in contradiction with other evidence this Chamber received. Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, in the Karadzic case, when you testified, you did correct some parts of your statement but you did not correct or clarify some of the portions of your statement that you have changed here today. Isn't it true that you have made those changes to the Karadzic statement after swearing in court in that case that your statement was truthful?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I personally believe that today, before this Chamber, there was more specific reference to this than in the Karadzic case. Perhaps it might seem that there are some differences there, but basically I stand behind what I said today as well as what I said in the Karadzic case. It is only that here we have been a bit more detailed on the subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, when you were asked, I believe two sessions ago - I think it was at temporary transcript page 3, although it may have been 5 - you were asked if asked the same questions today that you were asked in the statement you would give the same answer, your answer was actually, "I hope so." Is that because you know you have difficulty with the details and the information contained in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Today, when I speak after 22 years, it is only normal that there are some things that I cannot recall and that there are some consequences there. Perhaps I cannot recall some things I could recall a year and a half ago. But I cannot believe that everything that I said in the Karadzic case differs much from what I basically said today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, is it true that by May of 1992, Foca town was under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Foca town was under Serb control in May. In fact, it was under their control in the second half of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: There were several mosques in Foca before the war; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were mosques in Foca. There were active ones and there were others that were not at all used as places of worship because they were subjected to the ravages of time. Some were dilapidated; others were under state protection; yet others were used as enterprise premises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the simple question was whether there were mosques, several mosques. The answer apparently is yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there was a number of mosques.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Concerning your evidence -- and by the way, your testimony today regarding the NATO bombing resulting in the destruction of mosques, have you mentioned that evidence before?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: No. No, but that is because no one asked me about it. I cannot say that they were destroyed. They were damaged when the bridges were shelled, and tens of projectiles of high destructive power actually fell on those facilities, on all the bridges and the surrounding facilities including mosques which were all collateral damage. I did say that no shell hit the damage -- the mosques directly because they were shot shelling the mosques. That was not their target. No one in their right mind would think that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 13426. This is a collection of Council of Europe reports regarding the destruction of cultural heritage in the former Yugoslavia. Your Honours, it is not translated in part because we didn't have notice of this aspect of the witness's evidence, which I will use it to respond to.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Looking at the cover page, sir, once it comes up, we see the date of 2 February 1993. If we could turn to page 33, please, sir, here we see a list of destroyed mosques, and when we look at Foca, we see nine mosques listed. If we could turn to the top of the next page, we see additional destroyed mosques in Foca or the Foca region. So, sir, as of February 1993, the Council of Europe was already reporting a large number of destroyed mosques in Foca. Would you agree that this is long before the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, it was before and after. But if you will allow me to say why some of them were damaged and some of them were demolished --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: -- and perhaps it is superfluous for me to say --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: -- I simply asked you whether February of 1993 was before the NATO bombings and I believe your answer was yes. If we could now go to page 176, when it comes up, this will be a portion of a report dated the 19th of January 1994, also from the Council of Europe. And, sir, we read here in the middle of the page: "Before this war struck Foca, there were 13 admirable examples of Islamic sacral architecture to be found in this town. All of them suffered grave damage from shells, and after the town was captured, many of them were simply demolished." It's true that 13 mosques in Foca have been gravely damaged before the NATO bombing, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. That happened before and after. And there were mosques that even in the time of the pre-war Yugoslavia, before these conflicts, were damaged and were not at all used as places of worship but were used as storehouses for shops and for other purposes. But these facilities which were not used for their basic purpose existed also before, even prior to the Second World War, and were never reconstructed and they were used for other purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, we are talking about 13 of the mosques in Foca that were standing prior to the war, that were not standing by 1993; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly for how long they were in this condition, but if anything, they suffered the most damage during the conflicts in Foca, during -- between the Serb and Muslim forces. I've already told you before that the Muslims used such places of worship to open fire from them and to store their weaponry in them, and that they deliberately provoked the Serb forces so as to actually have portrayed to the international community that the Serbs were demolishing the places of worship of the Islamic community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, could I ask one question? You earlier answered the question I put to you about what was the shell coming closest to a mosque so as to damage it. Could you tell us it was closest to what mosque where you said it fell at 100 to 150 metres from a mosque, targeting the bridge, I think. Could you tell us which mosque you had on your mind at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The shells landed around the bridge, behind the bridge, at some distance from the bridge, and the nearest mosque was one which is not even 100 metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please give me the name of that mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Musluk in Donje Polje, and Cafe Bor mosque in Donje Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that in Foca town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Foca town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the names? You said Musluk.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: If the witness could please be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you come closer to the microphone and could you repeat the names of the mosques you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the lower bridge on the Drina was shelled, it was the Musluk mosque in Donje Polje which was not 150 metres away from the place the shells landed as the crow flies. I believe the other was the mosque which is called the mosque called Cafe Bor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Which might mean by the Bor cafe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, if we could modify our view on the page we are looking at to see the entire page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, witness, if you're talking about the Musluk mosque, then that mosque was already reported as being destroyed in 1993. Not damaged but destroyed. Do you have any explanation for --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, where are you seeing that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm seeing that on page 33 of the first -- of the Council of Europe report, where the -- I think Ms. Bibles has drawn our attention to 13 mosques reported as being destroyed. And we find there the mosque, the Musluk mosque, in the other report says Atik Alipasina? Mosque. We find Atik Alipasina mosque 1546, and that is the same date in the other report, being destroyed, that is two asterisks, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It says, "which it fears are damaged or destroyed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It says, "which it fears are damaged or destroyed." That's what the report says, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let me see.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At paragraph 112 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree that it says -- that's our problem with trying to digest the information immediately. What we see in the other report, that it's reported "suffered extensive damage in April 1992," and here, "it fears are damaged or destroyed." Well, I must say that the language "fears" is a bit unclear to me, a bit ambiguous. But I fully take your point, Mr. Ivetic, that it doesn't say -- yes. But there apparently was already considerable damage to that mosque. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with that, that the Musluk mosque was damaged and, for the most part, demolished in April 1992 because Muslim forces opened fire from there, and there was a recoilless gun which also opened fire from another direction where the Serb forces were, and that they hit the minaret. That mosque would not have been destroyed by NATO shells, but it could have been further damaged than it already was. Other mosques also suffered some damage from the bombardment, as did residential blocks and other buildings. All that was collateral damage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed. If the parties could agree in any way on where the Bor or close to the Bor cafe mosque is, which one is that in those reports, that would be appreciated. Ms. Bibles, I think you presented the list as "destroyed" and not that there was "fear that it was destroyed," which may have misled me slightly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I apologise for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Having pulled this document out while the witness was testifying, I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that by the end of the war, there were no minarets left in Foca municipality at all?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: No, there were some that were standing. At the end of the war, too. And today, in the city of Foca, there are still some structures that were damaged prior to the outbreak of the war conflict and they are still standing as such today.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, going to the destruction of one mosque, the Aladza mosque, you've already agreed that Foca town was under Serb control well before August of 1992 when the mosque was destroyed. Sir, isn't it true that even if there had been explosives in this mosque at the beginning of the conflict, by August of 1992, Serb forces had had several months to remove any such devices?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Perhaps they could take those explosives away. I did not go into the mosque to see what the quantity was. I only know that it was not demolished, that mosque, until August 1992. Someone - who, we don't know; they don't know whether it was an individual, was it groups, whether it was in retaliation - someone actually blew up that mosque and set the explosives on fire and it collapsed. But we know that someone could have done it to exact revenge because the very first shell which fell was on Serbs from the minaret.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, you're a lawyer and you understand the import of evidence. Is it clear or is it your testimony that you simply do not know what happened to that mosque, other than the fact that it was destroyed in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: It was destroyed in August 1992, but this was not organised by the civilian and military authorities but by individuals or some other groups or illegal groups which were able actually to mill about Foca because it was a mosque that was under state protection. It was not active. There were no services there. It was only at a later stage that the Islamic people actually gathered there for that purpose. But during the previous period, it was not an active place of worship.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I rise for a translation issue. Temporary transcript page 66, line 3, my colleague tells me that the witness did not say that it was the very first shell which fell, but I did not catch the B/C/S to be able to assist any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please then revisit that matter. Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, I now want to turn to a different direction. I want to ask you about your time standing guard at the facility where women were held in April of 1992. Who specifically told you to stand guard in that location?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: This was instructed by the Crisis Staff. There were individuals in Gornja Polje who designated me and somebody else, another person - I don't know who was later assigned after I was mobilised - but they assigned us to secure the facility because there were a number of women in the Partizan facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And just to make sure that we are clear, those were the only four days in which you were physically present at Partizan hall yourself.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: At night. At night. From morning till dusk, rifle in hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, apologies, but your observation about page 66, line 3, would that mean that we would need to seek verification of that portion of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Or ask the witness. Either way. I did not actually hear the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I suggested more or less to Ms. Bibles who then moved on to another subject. Perhaps it's better to have it clarified, Ms. Bibles, because otherwise once the translation has been verified, the witness might be back home.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, we are going back to the last topic and we want to make sure that we have captured your testimony correctly. Your testimony was, with respect to the mosque, "But we know that someone could have --" wait, that's not -- "but we know that someone could have done it to exact revenge because the very first shell which fell was on Serbs from the minaret." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I didn't say "shell." What I said was that there was an armed fighter of Muslim ethnicity who opened at passers-by. His name -- and somebody was hit there in the immediate vicinity, and the name of the hit person was Trifkovic. He was hit from the minaret of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not asking to further elaborate on it, but do we then understand that you wanted to say that someone could have done it to exact revenge because the first fire or fire was opened on Serbs from this minaret?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was not a shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just also point out something here. I don't know whether there was a -- on this second topic that you were talking about now, Ms. Bibles, the witness said he was keeping -- he was at those houses for those four days at night, and then it was interpreted from dawn to dusk. That seems to be a contradiction, dawn to dusk is in the day, and if it's at night, it would be dusk to dawn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So sir, just to clarify your testimony, you were there from dusk to dawn?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: That was a slip of the tongue, if that's what I said. It was from dusk until dawn, throughout the night. Without any break, without any replacements, throughout the night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, we are at the point where we should take a break. Witness, would you please follow the usher? Ms. Bibles, could you meanwhile tell us how much more time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I actually thought I was going to finish this session, but I certainly will finish in the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would expect, then, you to finish in the next session in ten or 15 minutes, but let's try to conclude at least the evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I am intending to do so, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But would there be sufficient time left for some re-examination, Mr. Ivetic? Could you give us any --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One question so a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the Bench may have some questions as well, so you're encouraged, Ms. Bibles, to see whether you can finish in anything between 15 and 20 minutes. We will take a break and we will resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be brought in, we briefly discussed what "it fears" means in the context of the report, if the parties would have any further explanations for that, other than it's just a way of saying, perhaps, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would direct you to page 33 where it says for the Aladza mosque, where it says "rumour in Sarajevo has it that the famous mosque was destroyed." So we are talking about rumours and hearsay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I would suggest is that we MFI this document, and perhaps Defence counsel and I, we may not be able to agree, but that we make submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least you have a look at it together and of course there is more evidence about it. I think we have Mr. Riedlmayer who testified about mosques, and I have no clear recollection of what exactly he said on these mosques. But, Ms. Bibles, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement referring to what we've ascertained is Partizan hall, you say, "All the women left this facility as far as I know no later than June 1992." Do you stand by that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I stand by that but perhaps even earlier, because they were there very briefly. They left with the other citizens who wanted to leave Foca. That is what they had the right to do. They expressed their own wish, their own willingness to do that, and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And sir, I want to clarify or, before we leave today, make sure that we understand. Is it accurate that Partizan hall is the only one of these facilities where Muslims were that you were present at during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: That facility was near the building where I lived. It was 150 metres away. However, since I was elderly at the time, I hadn't been mobilised, the Crisis Staff, through their commissioners, selected people who would carry out their duties conscientiously and stand guard by that facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, I want to make sure that we understand that this is the only one of these facilities in Foca that you were physically present at while Muslims were being held in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: That was the only facility, but there were also private houses where there were women in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Were you ever physically present at those private homes during 1992 where the women, other women, were being held in Foca?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Never, never. It never crossed my mind even.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could bring up P2822, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You've testified several times that people were free to leave Foca or that they had been given permission to leave Foca, and I'd like to clarify when that became true, sir. So when this document comes up, sir, this document is dated 18 June 1992. And this is the war commission decision in which the civilian -- it reads, in section 1: "The civilian and military authorities shall allow all loyal citizens who have not violated the laws of the Bosnian Serb Republic or done anything in the still-ongoing war to endanger the safety of the Serbian people in our area to leave in the direction of their choice." Sir, isn't it true that until 18 June 1992, people did not have the right to leave Foca?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, of course, as soon as the town of Foca became predominantly Serbian, all loyal citizens of Muslim ethnicity had the right to say whether they would leave or stay. And that's what they were told, and this order puts that very nicely, that they could stay. They were even persuaded to stay. As a matter of fact, the Serb population, it was not -- oh, yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that the order that you've been talking about and the ability to leave Foca began on 18 June 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what? In the month of April, whenever a citizen of Muslim ethnicity wanted to move out of Foca, they could, through Montenegro, Ustikolina, to Sarajevo, wherever they wanted to go. This document followed only later. I know that personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could now bring up 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you do that, before you do that, I would like to put to the witness the following: If you look at this document, I think it's the longer -- the third paragraph, there, it says: "The present civilian and military authorities of the Serbian Municipality of Foca have so far been preventing both Serbs and Muslims from leaving the Foca territory." How do you comment upon that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm trying to say is that this did not go for the civilian authorities, but the military authorities, they did not exist. It was only the Territorial Defence at the time. It was not desirable for any citizens to leave Foca, of any one of the three ethnic backgrounds. It was in the explicit interest for all the population to remain and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You just said before that the Muslims had the right to leave wherever they wanted to go even before the 18th of June. Now I read a part of this document to you that the authorities have so far been preventing both Serbs and Muslims from leaving the Foca territory. What is your comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say that they did not prevent anyone physically from leaving. Serbs and Muslims were leaving. I mean, half of my family left Foca in the month of April and went to Serbia. My son with his family went to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before the 18th of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, in April. That's when my son left, left Foca, that is, with a young child.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation as to why what the document says squarely contradicts what you're saying? Apart from an example you gave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this document sounds to me that none of the population should leave Foca, so that Foca would remain intact with a mixed population so that everybody would be there. That was the interest of that initial Serb authority in the municipality and town of Foca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did your family leave Foca? What date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Beginning of the month of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you be a bit more precise? Was it before the conflict broke out? That means before the 8th of April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it was getting obvious that there was this danger of a conflict breaking out in Foca, I recommended to my son that he leave with his three-month-old child - I will tell you this - to leave Foca and go to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop you here. No one asked you who advised your son to leave. What I was interested in, whether it was before the conflict broke out or after, and I do understand from your answer that it was -- please do not interrupt me. Please do not interrupt me. I do understand that it was before the conflict broke out. Thank you for your answer. Ms. Bibles, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few days, a few days, before the conflict broke out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop you. You've answered the question. Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Finally, if we could go to 65 ter 30984.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, this is a report from the Foca Tactical Group dated 31 August 1992. I'll have you look at point 5 which I believe will be on page 2 in the English version. Yes, if we could go to page 2 on the English version, please. Thank you. Sir, we see that this is a report from Colonel Marko Kovac, and it reads, on point 5: "Special. In the course of 30.8 we released from prison a total of 55 elderly, unfit Muslim males. On 31-08 we released 40 women and children, to keep a visiting commission from discovering them and as an alibi." Do you see that language?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: What I can say about the exchange, as for people leaving the KP Dom, that happened at one point in time. I don't know exactly when -- may I start?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, I simply asked to make sure that you were looking at the right language. My question is this: I understand that it's your evidence that women were detained in Foca --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, that women were detained in Foca for their own protection. If the VRS was detaining these women for their own protection, then why would Colonel Kovac have felt the need to keep a visiting commission from discovering them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Misstates the evidence as to who was keeping these women.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look exactly the -- of course, we -- by saying it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 4 of the witness's statement, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, the language I was looking at was the "we" in point 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I understood it as well, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, and the document is from the Centre for Information of Trebinje, not from the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, no one suggested that it was the VRS, at least I didn't hear that in Ms. Bibles's -- or was it, Ms. Bibles?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It was in the question; that's why I objected. If the VRS was detaining these women, that's why I objected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question will be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'll rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, I understand that your evidence has been that women were detained in Foca for their own protection. If these women were being detained for their own protection, why would Colonel Kovac have felt the need to keep a visiting commission from discovering them?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this document here right in front of me. I'm not aware of this, but I know that the women who were first received in Partizan, they went in a completely different way. Now, what group of women this is about, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree that Colonel Kovac by August of 1992 was with the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: That's what's written here, Marko Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further examination for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The last question was not answered. Sir, was Colonel Marko Kovac, in August -- end August 1992, an officer of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the Army of Republika Srpska was formed, Marko Kovac came to the helm of the command of the Army of Republika Srpska, when the Army of Republika Srpska was established, that is. But up until August, I mean, no, July, Marko Kovac did not appear. A bit before that, I think, he did appear. Well, that would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was he an officer of the VRS on the 31st of August 1992? This is my question. Nothing else. "Yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was an officer of the Army of Republika Srpska in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something. May I? I cannot? Nothing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the end of your testimony, if there is anything you would like to, but at this moment, Judge Moloto wanted to address Ms. Bibles, I think, and you're not supposed to interrupt him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you want to do with this 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 65 ter 30984.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We reject. The witness has not had any prior knowledge or been able to confirm the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you oppose against it to be bar tabled in direct relation to matters the witness testified about?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we, at the Defence, have been asked to cut down exhibits that we have that witnesses have actually talked about and knew about, so in that situation, I would ask that both sides be treated fairly. If we are cutting down documents that we have witnesses who testify about in their written statements as associated exhibits, then I think that the Prosecution should have documents introduced that are actually able to be verified by witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I don't have to remind you that if I ask a question, that I always prefer to get an answer to that question, and if you, for one reason or another, wanted to make a submission on the matter, then I would allow that. But my question is still without an answer, whether you would oppose, apart from whether you consider it at this moment appropriate to tender anything from the bar table, whether you would oppose this document which is in direct connection with portions of the evidence of this witness to be bar tabled.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My understanding of the rules for bar table are that there must be submissions made as to the authenticity of the source of the documents. We don't have that at this present --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us something about the source of this document, Ms. Bibles?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will take me a few moments. Perhaps we could MFI this and then come back to it before we leave the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will MFI it for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, the Chamber will admit the document into evidence. It is stamped. There are no specific challenges to the authenticity at this moment. Therefore the Chamber at this moment sees no reason not to admit it. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could I get a ruling, then, on my objection, Your Honour? I said that the heading of the document does not purport to what the document is. I said that earlier. I said it says, "The Republika Srpska Centre for Information Trebinje." Can I get a ruling on that objection on a document that's been tendered without a witness to testify as to its authenticity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked Madam Registrar to provide a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30984 receives number P6681, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Ivetic, you made an observation in relation to this document earlier. I think you did not specifically ask for any ruling on that at that moment. Second - and you interrupted me; otherwise you would have heard that from me anyhow - that if there is any specific reason to revisit the authenticity of this document, you have an opportunity to do so, and the Chamber would like then to receive a reasoned challenge to the authenticity of this document. I take it, Ms. Bibles, that you'll be prepared for that anyhow and tell us then where the document comes from.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is part of the Herzegovina Corps collection that came in to the OTP. I can provide -- well, I see Mr. Ivetic on his feet. I'll be prepared to respond, in answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's what I was wondering, whether I need to respond or whether I need to initiate any submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon? I'm sorry, I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm wondering whether I need to respond or initiate any submissions as to the authenticity of this document? Where does the burden lie?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Respond to what exactly, Mr. Ivetic? I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm understanding your decision, Your Honours, that's saying that I have to now present a submission as to the authenticity of a document for which I have not had any tender of anything from the Prosecution. I'm asking who has the burden to establish the authenticity of the document. I believe the party tendering it has that burden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there is no burden under the rules. The Chamber may require proof of authenticity. That is what the rule tells us, and I don't know whether I'm literally quoting but that's at least the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for that purpose, we have decided on the matter and we allowed the Defence to revisit any authenticity issue if it wishes to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And Mr. Ivetic, it was really a misstatement. The Presiding Judge clearly said on page 79, line 11 and 12, if there is any specific reason to revisit the authenticity of this document, you have an opportunity to do so. This is really different from what you were putting to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But how can the Defence make a submission about authenticity of a document without the party tendering it saying where they got the document from. It reverses the burden on the Defence for something -- we are not submitting the document, Your Honour, so why would we have to bear the burden of authenticating a document? That's why I was confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A document is tendered into evidence, a document which the Chamber, of course, has a look at its appearance. Meanwhile, we know from the Prosecution where it originates from, and you referred to the rule on who has to establish the authenticity. I referred you to what I now see as Rule 89, under (e), "A Chamber may request verification of the authenticity of evidence obtained out of court." On the basis of your submissions and on viewing the document and hearing that the Prosecution offered to give further information about the source, the Chamber refrained from requesting or ordering the Prosecution to give further information about the authenticity, but it left it open that the Defence may revisit that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In addition, Mr. Lukic, the legal position at this stage is that the Chamber has admitted the document. You're challenging that ruling of admission so therefore the burden to initiate is on you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's proceed. You have concluded your cross-examination. Mr. Ivetic, any questions on re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, the one that I had foreshadowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked by Judge Orie about Muslims that stayed in Foca, and at temporary transcript pages 47 through 48, were you shown paragraph 16 of your Karadzic statement which talked about many -- pardon me, of some Muslims that had fought in the VRS. Do you recall the names or positions of any of these VRS personnel who were Muslims from Foca?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, I can remember some. I've forgotten the names of some others. There was a Muminovic who was in the VRS. He was in charge of providing food to units who held positions on the line of separation, the administrative line of separation between Foca and Gorazde. There were Croats as well, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, again, sir for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's the only question I had in redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were there more Muslims than this Muminovic in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were more Muslims, and some people who hailed from mixed marriages also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But Muminovic is the only name you can tell us about a Muslim serving in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, I do remember this Muminovic. It was long ago. I cannot even recall his first name. But there certainly were Muslims. If you let me -- perhaps gave some me time, perhaps I could recall some names. But at this precise moment I cannot recall the exact names of all of them individually. There was a Muslim family which was loyal and in the formation throughout the war, from a mixed marriage of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you used the word "loyal" and that is a word that is used in some of the documents as well. What do you understand exactly by "loyal"? Is it that they have to commit themselves to the Serb --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Meaning that they accepted all the rules and the standards and norms relative to the state, relative to the authorities, that were also accepted by Serbs. This is what I mean by loyalty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: But it was not as if they were blackmailed to the effect of "You have to accept this or that." That was not that kind of loyalty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if they would oppose Serb rule but -- not taking up arms but, well, let's say politically try to change the situation, would those be considered to be loyal or would those considered not to be loyal?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Precisely during the war, no one actually forbade the SDA to pursue the policy of the Muslim people. No one prohibited them from doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that was not my question. But if they would pursue a change of government, a change of local government, not accepting that the Serb rule should apply, would they be considered loyal or would they not be considered to be loyal?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, it is a democratic right for one to declare one's views and opinions and to pursue a specific policy. I do not think that such citizens would have to bear any consequences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Because there were people of Serb ethnicity also who actually sided with some other parties and there were mutual conflicts arising between them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This brings me to my next question. Was the Serb rule in Foca established by democratic principles?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what was the moment that the democratic decision-making in the municipality of Foca was adopted?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: The democratic process was based on the decisions of the highest organ of the -- organs of the Municipal Assembly and it was equal vis-à-vis all citizens who lived there. That's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were Muslims still participating in that decision-making?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: If they were elected, yes, they were participating. I do not know specifically that anyone was elected because they were in a minority there after the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before the war broke out, who decided democratically at what moment exactly that Serb rule would apply?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: When the Assembly of the Serbian People was founded in the area of the municipality and started issuing their regulations, that is how it happened, and that was immediately prior to the outbreak of the war. It was much later than this -- when this happened at the republican level because the municipalities were always late in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was the Assembly of the Serbian People established by a democratic vote among the citizens of Foca?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Before the outbreak of the war, it was known who the Serb Assemblymen were, and these assemblymen who were elected democratically by democratic vote of the parties to be members of the assembly, they were the ones who comprised the Municipal Assembly of Foca municipality. So they were elected in a democratic way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but it was only the Serb assemblymen elected that later formed the Assembly of the Serbian People.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, but -- yes, but those of other ethnicity who were not elected democratically were not assemblymen before the war, could not comprise part of that municipality. Had there been a Muslim assemblyman who Foca who had been elected prior to this period democratically, he would have become a member of this assembly too. There were Montenegrins, there were Croats, who were assemblymen. At the helm of the assembly was Milicic, Danilo Milicic. He was the president of the assembly. He was a Montenegrin. He was democratically elected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And he then became a member of the Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was elected prior to the war to the Serbian Assembly, and he was the president of the assembly. And later, when it actually set a part, he became the president of the Serbian Assembly of the municipality and discharged that particular duty for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I leave it to that for the moment. I have a few more questions for you. Do you know anything about, from personal observation, about arming of Serbs in Foca?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, I have some partial knowledge about this. Both the Serbs and the Muslims armed themselves in different ways. The Serbs began to do that late, with the assistance of multiple sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't want general information. I would like to know if you have any personal knowledge that is based on personal observation.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I know that people actually did what they can in different ways privately to get hold of arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not what I consider personal observation but, rather, a general statement. Do you have any specific knowledge about the fate and, again, personal observation about the fate of those who were detained in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: I have no knowledge whatsoever about the KP Dom. I cannot say anything about it. I cannot say either "yes" or "no" or it was like this or it was like that, because I really knew nothing about who was detained there. I only know that some elderly people had been received into this KP Dom, this penal and correctional facility, and that there they were treated if a wholly different fashion than the prisoners prior to the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, you have no personal observation about it, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. I really cannot say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I said that at the very end of your testimony you would be given an opportunity to add anything to answers you gave, not to make general statements. But if there is any specific question where you think you should have added something that you were not allowed to do before, you may do it now.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VUJICIC
utterances.text: This is all I wanted to say. When I was talking about places of worship of the Islamic community, I want to say that all this happened during the conflict in April, and I'm a bit surprised that nobody asked me about what happened to Serb, Serbian places of worship, the churches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we leave it usually to the parties to ask questions and to consider what is relevant for this case or not. Ms. Bibles, I think I was the last one who put questions to the witness. Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, I think not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this concludes your evidence, Mr. Vujicic, and I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague, a long way for you, and for having answered the -- I start again because I see you had taken off your ear-phones already. I would like to thank you for coming to The Hague, which is a long way for you, and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for being very fair in hearing what I had to say. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day. Ms. Bibles?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: With respect to the 65 ter 13426, I believe we agreed to MFI that document, and Mr. Ivetic and I would attempt to reach some sort of agreement as to whether -- there were certain agreements about that, but I would ask that that be MFIed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think I have forgotten, or at least I have failed to ask for a number for it. Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 13426 receives number P6682, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6682 is admitted into -- is marked for identification. We adjourn for the day and we will resume tomorrow, Friday, the 18th of July, 9.30 in the morning, in this same Courtroom I.
